title: Chapter 52 — Outreach Sequences
intro: The multi-touch sequences that turn cold prospects into warm meetings across builder, designer, and contractor channels.

sections.title: The Builder Sequence
sections.content:
Touch 1 (Day 0): Phone call with a specific reference to their current project. Leave a voicemail if no answer — mention the project by name. Touch 2 (Day 2): Email with your spec package at three price tiers. Subject: 'Appliance packages for [project/company name].'

Touch 3 (Day 7): LinkedIn connection request with a personalized note. Touch 4 (Day 14): Value-add email — a manufacturer rebate announcement, a new product launch, or a code update relevant to their projects. Touch 5 (Day 30): Drop by a job site with your card and a spec sheet. 'I was in the neighbourhood and wanted to introduce myself in person.'

If no response after 5 touches, move to quarterly check-ins. They are not ready now. They may be in 6 months.

sections.title: The Designer Sequence
sections.content:
Designers respond to visual and relational outreach differently than builders. Touch 1: email with a portfolio-style presentation of recent projects you supported. Show beautiful kitchens, not spec sheets. Touch 2: invitation to a private product viewing or showroom evening.

Touch 3: share a relevant article or product launch — something that helps their work. Touch 4: NKBA event follow-up if you met them at an association meeting. Touch 5: offer a complimentary CEU (continuing education) session at your showroom.

Designers are won through education and aesthetic partnership, not through pricing pressure.

sections.title: Sequence Discipline
sections.content:
Log every touch in CRM. Set the next touch date before you close the current one. Never let a sequence die of neglect — either complete it or consciously park the account.

The data shows that 80 percent of trade accounts are won between touch 5 and touch 12. Most reps stop at touch 2. The rep who follows the full sequence has a structural advantage over every competitor who gives up early.
